title: A Ruined City Weeps Alone
overview: Jerusalem, destroyed by Babylon's army around 586 BC, is pictured as a grieving widow who mourns her losses, admits her wrongs and begs God to see her pain.

parts.label: The city like a widow (vv. 1-7)
parts.note: The once busy capital is pictured as a woman left alone, her people taken into exile, her festivals ended and her former allies (her "lovers") turned against her. She remembers her past glory while enemies laugh at her ruin.

parts.label: Shame and a looted temple (vv. 8-11)
parts.note: Pictures of a woman stripped bare and ritually unclean under the purity laws of the time show how low the city has fallen, as foreigners loot the temple and starving people trade treasures for bread. Twice the city breaks in with her own short cry, asking the LORD to look at her.

parts.label: "Is it nothing to you?" (vv. 12-16)
parts.note: The city's voice takes over, stopping passersby and describing God's anger as fire in her bones, a hunter's net, a yoke made of her own sins and a winepress where her young people are crushed like grapes. Christians have long read verse 12 as also fitting Jesus' suffering, though in context it is Jerusalem's cry.

parts.label: No one to comfort (vv. 17-19)
parts.note: The line "no one to comfort her" keeps returning, and here her neighbors shun her. The city admits the LORD is in the right and she rebelled, while her priests and leaders died searching for food.

parts.label: A plea to see and judge (vv. 20-22)
parts.note: She begs God to see her anguish, with the sword killing outside and famine and death inside. She ends by asking God to punish her gloating enemies as she has been punished, a raw cry with no tidy resolution.

disagreement: Readers differ on whether the poem fully accepts the city's suffering as deserved punishment, or also voices a quiet protest that the suffering went far beyond what any wrongdoing could justify.
think: When disaster comes partly through people's own choices, does admitting fault make the grief easier to carry, or harder?
